newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq raises taxes, cuts spending to steady dinar.
newsitem.headline: Iraq raises taxes, cuts spending to steady dinar.

text.p: Iraq's Central Bank is striving to maintain the value of the dinar against the dollar by strict monetary policies and tougher tax collection.

In newspaper remarks early this year Governor Isam Hweish vowed to continue with measures to restrain the money supply and improve methods of tax collection to withdraw as much money from circulation as possible.

In a cabinet meeting this month President Saddam Hussein told his ministers to stick to guidelines he issued last year urging them to rely on their own resources by trimming their bloated structures and by raising taxes for spending needs.

Money supply in Iraq is so tight that ministries now need approval from the presidential office for additional expenses. Printing of new money, apparently halted for about a year, is carried out only for projects of national interest.

Iraqis are also asked to pay an economic price for public services which were formerly offered at giveaway prices. Many are feeling the pinch of the taxman for the first time because the scope of revenue collection has been widened.
"You need the dinar to pay your taxes. You now need it in large quantities to pay for public utilities. You have to have it when needing other government services," said a Baghdad trader.
Reporting to the police station now costs money in Iraq. So do legal documents signed by notaries public. Traffic police now fine offenders on the spot.

The government is said to have revised a decades-old law under which landlords were not allowed to increase rents or evict tenants. Under the new law, rewritten mainly to increase tax revenues, tenants of commercial property will have to pay the market price and will be forced out if they fail to pay the new rents.

Under Saddam's measures the bloated public sector is compelled to become leaner. To meet deficits, ministries have embarked on a selling spree, offering vehicles, property, small factories and spare parts to the public.

"The government is trying its best to withdraw excess money from circulation. They are not saying how much they have collected but at least they are forcing us to stick to our dinars as we need them to pay their services," said another trader.

Another source of revenue for the government has been the tax of 400,000 dinars on trips abroad. For exemption from three-year-long compulsory military service the government now asks for 750,000 dinars.

Iraq's oil-for-food agreement with the United Nations has given a boost to the government's measures. The deal implemented on December 10 will throw more than $1.3 billion into Iraq's economy in six months in the form of food and medical supplies.
Traders said the deal would also free Iraq's trade ministry from the need to spend about $100 million a month on supplies for ration cards.

The oil deal and the government's anti-inflationary measures have boosted the value of the Iraqi dinar against the U.S. dollar. It now trades about 1,200 to the dollar compared with about 3,000 in January 1996.
